EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN – “The Regional Wage Incidence of Brazil’s 1990-94 Trade Liberalization”

====================================================================
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) combined with a shift-share (Bartik) treatment intensity.

Why appropriate
• The reform is a nation-wide policy whose timing is common to all regions; what varies is the intensity of the tariff cut each micro-region (r) receives, owing to its pre-reform industrial structure.  
• Industry-level tariff changes are plausibly exogenous to subsequent regional wage growth once we condition on (i) initial tariff levels and (ii) pre-reform regional characteristics.  
• Worker-level census micro-data give very large samples, allowing flexible fixed effects and clustered errors.

Basic estimating equation (worker i, region r, year t ∈ {1991, 2000})  
  log wage_irt = α + β (Post_t × TariffCut_r) + γ_r + δ_t + X’_irt θ + ε_irt

β captures the causal effect on wages of a one-point larger regional tariff cut (i.e., exposure-weighted percentage-point fall in tariffs).

====================================================================
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
TariffCut_r ≡ Σ_j s_rj,1987 × ΔTariff_j,1991-2000  
• s_rj,1987 = share of region r’s employment in industry j in 1987 (predetermined).  
• ΔTariff_j = change in nominal tariff rate for industry j between 1991 and 2000.  
It is a continuous “dose”; higher values imply larger local exposure.

Control group  
Regions in the bottom quartile of TariffCut_r are effectively the comparison group, but the design exploits the full continuous variation, not binary treatment.

Treatment timing  
Post_t = 1 in 2000 census, 0 in 1991 census. (We will check robustness using 1980 PNAD or census to test for pre-trends.)

No running variable/cut-off: not an RDD design.

====================================================================
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel Trends: In the absence of trade liberalization, high- and low-exposure micro-regions would have experienced the same wage growth.  
Plausibility: Before 1990 tariffs were quasi-fixed for years; no contemporaneous policy clearly correlated with pre-1987 industrial composition. Can be probed with 1980–1991 placebo trends.

A2. Exogeneity of Tariff Changes Conditional on Initial Tariffs: Industry tariff cuts are driven by national political economy, not by region-specific shocks correlated with wages.  
Plausibility: Cuts were steeper where ex-ante protection was highest (mechanical); controlling for initial tariffs and their interaction with region shares helps.

A3. Stable Industry Share Weights: 1987 employment shares are predetermined and not affected by future shocks.  
Plausibility: 1987 predates reform; no evidence of anticipatory reallocation that early.

A4. No General-Equilibrium Spillovers across Micro-regions that Differ Systematically with TariffCut_r Beyond Captured by Aggregate Time FE.  
Plausibility: Some migration or goods-market spillovers exist; we will show results are robust to net migration controls and state-by-year fixed effects.

====================================================================
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION AND RESPONSES
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential pre-trends in high-protection regions.  
 • Response: Plot and estimate event-study coefficients using 1980 census or 1983–1989 PNAD; include region-specific linear trends; exclude outlier regions.

T2. Concurrent regional policies correlated with industrial structure (e.g., state privatizations, regional development programmes).  
 • Response: Add state-year fixed effects; control for changes in public-sector employment shares, FDI inflows, and infrastructure spending where available.

T3. Migration selectively redistributes workers across regions, biasing wages.  
 • Response: (i) Compute results on place-of-birth subsample (stayers).  
  (ii) Control for net in-migration rate 1991-2000.  
  (iii) Show that results are similar when using average firm-level wages from RAIS data (if obtainable) which attach to the job rather than the worker.

====================================================================
5. R CODE OUTLINE
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
#--------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Libraries
#--------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast fixed-effects regression
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

#--------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data loading
#--------------------------------------------------------------
# Assume three csv files: tariffs.csv, emp87.csv, workers.csv
# tariffs: industry, tariff_1991, tariff_2000
# emp87  : micro, industry, emp87
# workers: worker-level census extract 1991 & 2000

tariffs  <- fread("tariffs.csv")           # industry id
emp87    <- fread("emp87.csv")             # micro, industry, emp87
workers  <- fread("workers.csv")           # worker microdata

#--------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct tariff change per industry
#--------------------------------------------------------------
tariffs[, dTariff := tariff_2000 - tariff_1991]

#--------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Build region-level exposure TariffCut_r
#--------------------------------------------------------------
# merge employment shares
emp87    <- merge(emp87, tariffs, by = "industry")

# compute regional employment totals
emp87[, total_emp := sum(emp87), by = micro]
emp87[, share87   := emp87 / total_emp]

# regional tariff exposure
reg_expo <- emp87[, .(TariffCut = sum(share87 * dTariff)), by = micro]

#--------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Merge exposure into worker file
#--------------------------------------------------------------
workers <- merge(workers, reg_expo, by = "micro")

# create Post dummy
workers[, post := ifelse(year == 2000, 1, 0)]

# log wage
workers[, lwage := log(monthly_earnings / 4.33 / weekly_hours)]

#--------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Controls
#--------------------------------------------------------------
workers[, `:=`(
   age2  = age^2,
   female = sex == "F",
   married = marital == "Married"
)]

#--------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Main DID regression
#--------------------------------------------------------------
did_main <- feols(lwage ~ post * TariffCut + age + age2 + female +
                    race + married + factor(education) + factor(industry) |
                    micro + year,
                  data = workers,
                  cluster = ~ micro)

summary(did_main)

#--------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. Robustness: region-specific linear trends
#--------------------------------------------------------------
workers[, trend := ifelse(year == 2000, 1, 0)]   # with only 2 years this = post
did_trends <- feols(lwage ~ post * TariffCut + post:trend +  # implicit trend
                    age + age2 + female + race + married |
                    micro + year,
                    data = workers,
                    cluster = ~ micro)
summary(did_trends)

#--------------------------------------------------------------
# 8. Event-study placebo using 1980 vs 1991 (if data available)
#--------------------------------------------------------------
# ... analogous code omitted for brevity ...
```

====================================================================
6. EXPECTED RESULTS
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory (specific-factor & Heckscher-Ohlin models) predicts that falling tariffs in an import-competing sector reduce the rental to the sector-specific factor and, with imperfect inter-regional factor mobility, depress local wages. Therefore:

• Direction: β < 0. Regions whose weighted tariff dropped by 10 p.p. should experience lower real wage growth than otherwise similar regions.

• Magnitude: Prior papers suggest roughly a 1:4 pass-through; a 10 p.p. larger tariff cut may reduce nominal wages by ≈2 percent (β ≈ −0.002 per percentage-point).

====================================================================
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DID)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Common pre-trends …… 0.7 (looks plausible but must be tested).  
C2: No anticipation ……… 0.8 (reform was sudden, little evidence of pre-emptive migration).  
C3: No differential shocks … 0.6 (possible concurrent policies—mitigated with controls).  
C4: Stable composition …… 0.7 (migration a concern but robustness planned).  
C5: SUTVA (no spillovers) … 0.6 (general-equilibrium effects could spill across regions).

Average ≈ 0.68 – acceptable but results must be interpreted with care.
